title: DNS Queries over HTTPS (DoH)
subtitle: Carrying every DNS question and answer inside an ordinary HTTPS request
summary: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) defines how a DNS client sends a query to a recursive resolver as an HTTP request and reads the DNS answer from the HTTP response. Each query-response pair becomes one HTTP exchange over https, so TLS protects it from eavesdropping and tampering. The DNS message itself is unchanged: the body is the same binary format that RFC 1035 defines, labelled with the media type application/dns-message.

eli5.summary: Asking a computer for a website's address used to be like shouting a question across a crowded room, where anyone could hear or change it. DoH puts the question in a sealed envelope and sends it through the same mail slot everyone else uses, so nobody in between can read it.

questions: is doh the same as dns over tls
why use dns id 0 in doh

tldr.problem: Classic DNS travels in the clear over UDP and TCP port 53, so on-path devices can watch, block or rewrite lookups, and web applications have no safe way to ask DNS questions.
tldr.mechanism: The client is configured with a URI Template and sends each binary DNS message to that HTTPS URL, either as a base64url dns query variable (GET) or as the raw request body (POST). The server replies with a 200 and a DNS message in the body.
tldr.outcome: DNS lookups get TLS confidentiality and server authentication, share port 443 with other web traffic, and inherit HTTP features such as caching, proxying and content negotiation.

sections.title: Introduction and goals
sections.content:
RFC 8484 defines DNS over HTTPS, or DoH, for sending DNS queries (RFC 1035) and getting DNS responses over HTTP (RFC 7540) using https URIs (RFC 2818). Because the URIs are https, TLS (RFC 8446) provides integrity and confidentiality. Each DNS query-response pair is mapped into one HTTP exchange.

The RFC says the approach is "more than a tunnel over HTTP". It sets default media types for requests and responses but uses ordinary HTTP content negotiation, and it aligns with HTTP caching, redirection, proxying, authentication and compression.

Two use cases drove the design: preventing on-path devices from interfering with DNS operations, and letting web applications reach DNS information through existing browser APIs in a way consistent with Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS). The document focuses on communication between DNS clients, such as an operating system stub resolver, and recursive resolvers. A server that speaks this protocol is a "DoH server" and a client is a "DoH client".

DoH does not change DNS itself. Names, record types and response codes behave exactly as before; only the carrier changes.
sections.eli5: DNS is the phone book that turns names into numbers. DoH keeps the phone book the same but changes how you call it: instead of a loud public speaker, you use the normal private web connection.

sections.title: Choosing a DoH server
sections.content:
A DoH client is configured with a URI Template (RFC 6570) that says how to build the URL for resolution, for example https://dnsserver.example.net/dns-query{?dns}. How the template is configured, discovered or updated is out of scope. It may be typed in by a user or supplied automatically, for instance in responses from DHCP or a similar protocol. A server MAY support more than one template, so different endpoints can offer different authentication requirements or service levels.

The server's identity is checked the way HTTPS always checks it, as defined in RFC 2818.

A DoH client MUST NOT use a different URI just because it was found outside its configuration, such as through HTTP/2 server push, or because a server offers an unsolicited response that looks like a valid answer. DoH does not extend resolution privileges to URIs the client does not recognize as configured.

This rule keeps the choice of who answers your DNS questions in the hands of the client's configuration rather than whichever web server happens to reply.
sections.eli5: You decide which helper answers your questions, and you write down their address ahead of time. If a stranger shouts an answer you did not ask them for, you ignore it.

sections.title: The HTTP request
sections.content:
A DoH client encodes a single DNS query into an HTTP request using either GET or POST. DoH servers MUST implement both. The template is processed without variables for POST. For GET, the single variable dns holds the DNS request message encoded with base64url (RFC 4648), with padding characters omitted.

POST
The raw DNS message is the request body, with Content-Type: application/dns-message. Requests are generally smaller than their GET equivalents.
GET
The message is base64url-encoded into the dns query variable. This is friendlier to many HTTP cache implementations.

The client SHOULD send an Accept header, and MUST be prepared to process application/dns-message responses whatever it says. To maximize cache friendliness, clients using media types that include the DNS header ID field SHOULD use a DNS ID of 0 in every request, since HTTP already correlates request and response. A varying ID would make semantically identical queries cache separately.

The RFC's example GET for www.example.com uses the path /dns-query?dns=AAABAAABAAAAAAAAA3d3dwdleGFtcGxlA2NvbQAAAQAB; the same query as a POST has a 33-byte body.
sections.eli5: You can hand over your question written on a slip pushed into the URL (GET), or inside the envelope itself (POST). Both work; the server has to understand both.

sections.title: The HTTP response and errors
sections.content:
Each DNS request-response pair maps to one HTTP exchange, and responses may be processed and transported in any order using HTTP's multi-streaming. The response body is a DNS message with media type application/dns-message. A DoH server MUST be able to process that type in requests.

The error model separates two layers. A successful 2xx HTTP status is used for any valid DNS response, regardless of the DNS response code, so even SERVFAIL or NXDOMAIN arrive with a 2xx. Non-successful HTTP statuses do not carry a reply to the DNS question; the client treats them like any HTTP client would. It might retry the same server after an authorization failure (401), or try a different server after an unsupported media type (415) or when the server cannot produce a suitable representation (406).

In the RFC's example, an IN AAAA query for www.example.com returns status 200, content-length = 61, cache-control = max-age=3709 and one answer record, 2001:db8:abcd:12:1:2:3:4, with a TTL of 3709 seconds.

HTTP status describes whether the exchange worked. The DNS response code inside the body describes whether the name exists.
sections.eli5: If the server answers "that name does not exist", the delivery still went fine, so it comes back as a normal successful reply. Only if the delivery itself breaks do you get a web error.

sections.title: The application/dns-message payload
sections.content:
The payload is a single DNS message in the on-the-wire format of Section 4.2.1 of RFC 1035, which refers to the full format in its Section 4.1. RFC 1035 limits UDP messages to 512 bytes, later updated by RFC 6891; this media type restricts the maximum DNS message size to 65535 bytes.

This is not the framing used by DNS over TLS (RFC 7858), which adds the two length bytes from Section 4.2.2 of RFC 1035. In DoH, HTTP supplies the length, so there are no length prefix bytes.

Clients MAY include one or more EDNS options (RFC 6891) in the request. Servers using this type MUST ignore the EDNS UDP payload size value in requests. For GET the payload is base64url encoded with no padding; for POST it is used directly as the body. The RFC registers application/dns-message with IANA as a binary format with intended usage COMMON, with the IESG as change controller.

All DoH clients and servers MUST support this type. Other media types are allowed through normal HTTP negotiation, but they must be able to express every DNS query that could be sent over UDP, except those needing multiple responses.
sections.eli5: The envelope holds exactly the same DNS letter as before, just not chopped into extra pieces. The web connection already knows where the letter ends.

sections.title: HTTP integration and caching
sections.content:
DoH MUST be used with the https URI scheme. A DoH exchange can pass through a hierarchy of both HTTP caches and DNS caches. Generic HTTP caches do not understand DNS, so servers must take care with the caching headers on GET responses. Responses to POST are not cacheable unless specific headers are sent, which is not widely implemented and not advised for DoH.

Servers SHOULD set an explicit freshness lifetime so that intermediaries do not invent their own heuristic. That lifetime MUST be less than or equal to the smallest TTL in the Answer section; equal to the smallest TTL is RECOMMENDED. With RRset TTLs of 30, 600 and 300, the freshness lifetime should be 30 seconds (Cache-Control: max-age=30). If the Answer section is empty and there is an SOA record in the Authority section, the lifetime MUST NOT exceed the SOA MINIMUM field (RFC 2308).

Clients MUST account for the Age header when computing DNS TTLs: a TTL of 600 with Age 250 leaves 350 seconds. HTTP/2 (RFC 7540) is the minimum RECOMMENDED HTTP version, because DNS needs reordering, parallelism, priority and header compression to stay competitive; earlier versions work semantically but may perform poorly.

Server push needs extra care: before using pushed data, the client MUST establish that the pushed URI is one it would itself have queried.
sections.eli5: Answers can be remembered for a while so nobody has to ask twice. The label on the answer must never say "keep this" for longer than the DNS answer itself allows.

sections.title: Privacy and security considerations
sections.content:
On the wire, DoH encrypts DNS traffic and requires authentication of the server, which mitigates passive surveillance and active attacks that divert DNS to rogue servers. DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) offers similar protection, while plain UDP and TCP transports are exposed. Using port 443 and mixing DoH with other HTTPS traffic can deter on-path interference and make traffic analysis harder. Padding guidance appears in RFC 8467.

In the server, the DNS wire format has no client identifiers, but the layers beneath and around it do. The client IP address, long-lived TCP connections, TCP Fast Open cookies, TLS session resumption, HTTP cookies, and header fields such as User-Agent and Accept-Language can all help correlate queries. The RFC advises exposing the minimal data needed and says HTTP cookies SHOULD NOT be accepted by DoH clients unless a use case requires them.

HTTPS does not provide the response integrity that DNSSEC provides. The RFC states that DNSSEC and DoH are independent, compatible protocols and that using one does not diminish the need for the other.

Because the transport is HTTP, classic UDP amplification attacks are mitigated.
sections.eli5: The sealed envelope hides your question from people along the road, but the post office at the end still sees who sent it. And a sealed envelope does not prove the answer inside is true; that is DNSSEC's job.

viz.caption: The DNS header that opens every application/dns-message body

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Query identifier. DoH clients SHOULD send 0 so equivalent queries share cache entries.

fields.name: QR
fields.desc: 0 for a query, 1 for a response.

fields.name: Opcode
fields.desc: Kind of query; 0 is a standard query.

fields.name: RD
fields.desc: Recursion desired. Set in the example query.

fields.name: RCODE
fields.desc: Response code, such as NXDOMAIN. Carried inside a 200 OK.

layers.label: HTTP
layers.detail: GET or POST, caching, content negotiation (HTTP/2 recommended)

layers.label: TCP
layers.detail: Port 443, shared with other HTTPS traffic

layers.label: IP
layers.detail: Client address remains visible to the server

today: DoH is widely deployed: major web browsers can resolve names over DoH, and several public resolver operators offer DoH endpoints. Operating systems and stub resolvers also ship client support. The core exchange remains the one in this RFC.
